Magma Series: Tholeiitic, Calc-Alkaline, and Alkaline

Dr. Ahmad Redaa

19-10-2025

What is a Magma Series?

Definition:
> A magma (igneous) series is a group of rocks related by chemical evolution and crystallization trends from a common parent magma.

Different series reflect:
- Source composition
- Degree of partial melting
- Crystallization path
- Tectonic setting

Major series:
1. Tholeiitic 2. Calc-Alkaline 3. Alkaline

Chemical Basis of Magma Series

  • Defined mainly by FeO–MgO–Alkali (Na₂O + K₂O) trends.
  • Illustrated by the AFM Diagram (Irvine & Baragar, 1971).

AFM Diagram Axes:
- A = Na₂O + K₂O (alkalis)
- F = FeO + Fe₂O₃ (iron)
- M = MgO (magnesium)

Trend Differences:
- Tholeiitic: strong Fe enrichment
- Calc-Alkaline: limited Fe enrichment, early Fe oxidation
- Alkaline: high alkali enrichment (Na + K)

1. Tholeiitic Series

Characteristics:
- Iron-rich trend on AFM diagram
- Common in mid-ocean ridges (MORB) and intraplate basalts
- Typically low Na₂O + K₂O
- High Fe/Mg ratio during fractionation
- Late-stage Fe–Ti oxide crystallization

Typical Minerals:
- Plagioclase (calcic → sodic)
- Clinopyroxene and orthopyroxene
- Olivine (early)
- Fe–Ti oxides (late)

Tectonic Setting:
- Oceanic ridges
- Intraplate basaltic provinces
- Some continental flood basalts

2. Calc-Alkaline Series

Characteristics:
- Moderate Fe enrichment (Fe oxidation to magnetite)
- Higher Al₂O₃ and CaO; lower FeO than tholeiitic series
- Common in volcanic arcs (subduction zones)
- Typically water-rich magmas → early crystallization of amphibole and biotite

Mineralogy:
- Plagioclase
- Clinopyroxene
- Amphibole, biotite
- Magnetite (oxidized Fe)

Tectonic Setting:
- Convergent plate boundaries (island arcs, continental arcs)

Examples:
Andesitic volcanoes of the Andes, Japan, Cascades

3. Alkaline Series

Characteristics:
- High Na₂O + K₂O and often high TiO₂
- Fe enrichment less pronounced
- Late-stage alkali feldspar and feldspathoid minerals (e.g., nepheline, leucite)
- Derived from low-degree partial melting of mantle source

Mineralogy:
- Alkali feldspar
- Nepheline, leucite (in undersaturated varieties)
- Clinopyroxene (Ti-rich)
- Olivine (commonly present)

Tectonic Setting:
- Intraplate or rift-related magmatism
- Hot spots, continental rifts

Examples:
Mount Kenya (East African Rift), Canary Islands, Ocean Island Basalts (OIB)

Comparison Summary

Feature Tholeiitic Calc-Alkaline Alkaline
SiO₂ (wt%) 45–60 55–70 40–60
Fe trend Strong Fe enrichment Moderate Fe (oxidized early) Variable
Na₂O + K₂O Low Moderate High
Water content Dry Wet Variable
Oxygen fugacity (fO₂) Low (reducing) High (oxidizing) Low–moderate
Tectonic setting Ocean ridges, intraplate Subduction zones Rifts, hot spots
Key rocks Basalt, gabbro Andesite, dacite Trachyte, phonolite
Example location Iceland, Hawaii Andes, Japan East African Rift

Geochemical Indicators

AFM Diagram Trends

  • Tholeiitic: FeO enrichment → MgO decrease
  • Calc-Alkaline: Alkali rise early; Fe constant or decreases
  • Alkaline: Alkalis dominate early, divergent trend

TAS Diagram (Total Alkalis vs. Silica)

  • Differentiates subalkaline (Tholeiitic + Calc-Alkaline) from alkaline series.
  • Boundary line by Irvine & Baragar (1971).

AFM Diagram
> A ternary diagram showing chemical evolution of igneous rocks based on A = (Na₂O + K₂O), F = (FeO + Fe₂O₃), and M = (MgO).

It is used to:
- Distinguish Tholeiitic, Calc-Alkaline, and Alkaline magma series.
- Display iron enrichment trends during fractional crystallization.
- Indicate oxidation state and water content of magmas.

Components of the AFM Diagram

Symbol Oxide Component Geological Meaning
A Na₂O + K₂O Alkalis — late-stage differentiation
F FeO + Fe₂O₃ Iron — redox and fractionation indicator
M MgO Early ferromagnesian crystallization

Axes:
- Triangular (ternary) plot normalized to 100%.
- Basalts and related rocks typically plotted.

Typical AFM Diagram (schematic)

The AFM diagram, a ternary diagram between the Alkali, Fe, and Mg oxides used to distinguish the calc-alkaline magma series from the tholeiitic magma series.
Key/Legend: A – alkali (sodium and potassium) oxides, F – iron oxides, M – magnesium oxide, BT – tholeiitic basalt, FB – ferro-basalt, ABT – tholeiitic basaltic andesite, AT – tholeiitic andesite, D – dacite, R – rhyolite, B – basalt, AB – basaltic andesite, A – andesite; dashed line – boundary between tholeiitic and calc-alkaline compositions.

Source: Wikimedia Commons

Interpretation:
- Tholeiitic trend: Moves from M → F → A (iron enrichment).
- Calc-Alkaline trend: Direct M → A, bypassing strong Fe enrichment.
- Alkaline series: Starts near A corner; higher Na + K content from the start.

What is the TAS Diagram?

TAS = Total Alkali vs. Silica Diagram

A geochemical classification chart that uses SiO₂ (wt%) and Total Alkalis (Na₂O + K₂O wt%)
to distinguish and name volcanic rocks (IUGS 1989).

It is used primarily for:
- Chemical classification of volcanic rocks (especially fine-grained).
- Differentiating subalkaline (tholeiitic + calc-alkaline) and alkaline rock series.
- Comparing magma compositions across tectonic settings.

Axes and Variables

Axis Parameter Represents
X-axis SiO₂ (wt%) Silica content — degree of differentiation
Y-axis Na₂O + K₂O (wt%) Total alkalis — sodium and potassium enrichment

Silica increases → differentiation
Alkalis increase → fractionation / partial melting influence

Fields on the TAS Diagram

TAS diagram showing chemical composition range of sub-alkaline volcanic rocks including calc-alkaline rocks (yellow area) and alkaline volcanic rocks (blue area).

Source: Wikipedia

The TAS diagram contains named compositional fields (Le Bas et al., 1986; IUGS, 1989):

Silica Range Alkalinity Field Common Rock Names
< 45% Basaltic fields Basalt, Basanite
45–52% Basaltic-andesitic fields Basaltic andesite, Trachybasalt
52–63% Intermediate fields Andesite, Trachyandesite
63–69% Felsic fields Dacite, Trachyte
> 69% High-silica fields Rhyolite, Phonolite

Dividing Line:
- The Irvine & Baragar (1971) line separates Subalkaline from Alkaline magmas.

Key Points:
- The x-axis increases with differentiation (SiO₂).
- The y-axis increases with alkali enrichment (Na₂O + K₂O).
- Alkaline rocks plot above the dividing line.
- Subalkaline rocks plot below the line.

Subalkaline vs. Alkaline Series

Feature Subalkaline (Tholeiitic + Calc-Alkaline) Alkaline Series
Total Alkalis Low to moderate High (Na + K enriched)
SiO₂ Moderate to high Variable
Mineralogy Plagioclase, pyroxene, amphibole Alkali feldspar, nepheline, leucite
Tectonic Setting Mid-ocean ridges, subduction arcs Intraplate rifts, hot spots
Examples Andesite, Dacite, Rhyolite Trachyte, Phonolite

Tectonic Associations Summary

Tectonic Environment Typical Magma Series Example Volcanoes
Mid-ocean ridge Tholeiitic Iceland, Atlantic Ridge
Island arc / continental arc Calc-Alkaline Andes, Japan, Cascades
Intraplate / continental rift Alkaline East African Rift, Canary Islands
